title: Gwalior stone, granite & marble: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What this business physically is
**Gwalior's stone units buy rough blocks, cut and polish them into slabs and tiles, and sell into construction demand — cash comes back only after the slab is sold and the buyer pays.** The value sits in the finished slab, not the block; the block is the working-capital sink. Capex is polishing lines and cutting equipment, largely imported — so a proposal landing with new imported machinery needs the landed cost and the supplier quote, collect from customer. Peer Aro runs 7.35 lakh sq m of slab and 3.60 lakh sq m of tile capacity [10] — use that as the scale yardstick when a Gwalior unit claims capacity. Nationally, IIP for NIC 23 is +11.4% YoY and +10.2% Apr-to-date [D], but bank credit is running +18.2% YoY against that output [D] — so the sector is being financed faster than it is producing. Madhya Pradesh GST is -0.1% Apr-to-date against India +6.1% [D], a local demand signal that is weaker than the headline. Peer evidence is mixed: Midwest grew 1QFY27 revenue 35% YoY [5] while Aro's June 2026 quarter net sales fell 23.72% YoY to Rs 20.62 crore [6]. Rating reports flag high European revenue concentration as a constraint [9] — that is exactly Gwalior's exposure. ## Where to grow
**Pursue domestic-facing processors selling into MP and North India construction, and units with quarry linkage or assured block supply.** Aro's ratings note proximity to raw material and group-owned quarries meeting around 40% of requirement as a strength [11] — look for that in Gwalior proposals. Avoid pure export-order units with European books until freight normalises [3], and avoid traders who hold no processing asset. Note plainly: the sources say almost nothing about Gwalior's stone cluster specifically beyond the export crisis [3]; the rest is first principles plus peers. ## How to grow safely
**Structure against the block-to-slab cycle, not the balance sheet.** Take monthly stock statements and a slab-wise inventory ageing; if finished-goods days rise while sales fall, ask for the buyer-wise order book. Take receivables ageing every month — if beyond-90-day debtors cross a third of book, stop enhancement. Peer Midwest's blended granite ASP was INR60,792/cbm [4] — ask each borrower for their realised price per cbm monthly and compare direction, not level. Rating reports show working-capital utilisation around 56% of sanctioned limits as comfortable [8]; treat sustained 90%+ utilisation as a warning, not a comfort. ## Early-warning signs
**Watch freight, order book and price together.** If a borrower reports European orders still on hold and asks for limit enhancement, decline and ask for domestic order evidence. If realised price per cbm falls two months running while inventory rises, cut exposure. If GST-local sales trend stays negative [D], tighten new-to-bank intake in Gwalior.
